title: The control of lateral stability during rapid stepping reactions evoked by antero-posterior perturbation: does anticipatory control play a role?
notes: It is proposed that the presence of an ML APA during compensatory stepping may represent an attempt to preplan a stereotypical stepping response, but that the ability to fully express the anticipatory phase is disrupted by the need to react rapidly to the unpredictable antero-posterior...

title: Proprioception from a spinocerebellar perspective.
notes: Develops the dorsal spinocerebellar tract system as a model showing that spinal proprioceptive processing produces a global representation of whole-limb parameters rather than a muscle-by-muscle or joint-by-joint code, with the functional organization originating in the biomechanical linkages of the limb and a distributed spinal processing network.
animal_study: Record dorsal spinocerebellar tract neurons during controlled multi-joint limb movements versus isolated joint rotations to test the whole-limb versus joint-by-joint coding framework.
robot_sim: Replace muscle-by-muscle proprioceptive feedback in a locomotor controller with a spinocerebellar-like whole-limb kinematic encoding stage, and test whether the global representation improves interjoint coordination and balance relative to a joint-by-joint representation.

title: Activation of groups of excitatory neurons in the mammalian spinal cord or hindbrain evokes locomotion
notes: Using Vglut2-ChR2 mice, photostimulation of either the lumbar spinal cord or the caudal hindbrain was sufficient to both initiate and maintain locomotor-like activity, directly demonstrating that glutamatergic neurons in the spinal cord are critical for initiating or maintaining the locomotor rhythm and that activation of hindbrain locomotor command regions can directly activate the spinal locomotor network.
animal_study: Silence Vglut2-positive spinal populations during ongoing locomotion, or sweep stimulation frequency and location, to dissociate the rhythmogenic versus command roles of spinal and hindbrain glutamatergic neurons.
robot_sim: Model locomotion initiation as a tonic excitatory glutamatergic drive channel that both starts and sustains the rhythm generator; ablating it should reproduce failure of locomotor initiation while leaving the remaining network structure intact.

title: Functional subpopulations of V3 interneurons in the mature mouse spinal cord.
notes: Identifies two physiologically and topographically distinct V3 interneuron subpopulations in the mature mouse spinal cord: ventral lamina-VIII cells with simple morphology and rapid tonic firing, active during running in a manner suggesting a premotor role, and dorsal cells with complex morphology, strong spike-frequency adaptation, large sag voltages and post-inhibitory rebound (consistent with HCN and T-type calcium currents), active during swimming in a manner suggesting a sensory-relay role.
animal_study: Separately silence ventral versus dorsal V3 subpopulations during running and swimming to causally test the premotor versus sensory-relay role assignments inferred from their task-dependent activity.
robot_sim: Split the commissural excitatory population in a CPG model into tonic-firing premotor and adapting rebound-capable relay subtypes with HCN- and T-type-like currents; test whether differential recruitment across gaits preserves rhythm robustness.

title: A spinal circuit for skilled locomotion
notes: Identifies V0g ascending neurons as a subtype of the V0 family integrated in lumbar sensorimotor circuits and specifically required for execution of the precise limb movements of skilled locomotion, revealing a previously unappreciated role for ascending spinal neurons in adjusting body movements to the demands of challenging locomotor tasks.
animal_study: Acute silencing of V0g ascending neurons during skilled versus simple locomotor tasks would test the behavioral specificity of the precision deficit, dissociating skill-level adjustments from basic walking.
robot_sim: Implement an ascending precision-correction pathway (V0g analog) that modulates limb-movement precision only in high-demand locomotion modes; ablate it in simulation and quantify loss of foot-placement precision on demanding terrain.

title: Effects of spinal transection and locomotor speed on muscle synergies of the cat hindlimb
notes: Fifteen hindlimb muscle EMGs in cats across 0.4–1.0 m/s before and after low-thoracic transection factor into five synergies in every condition; synergy number, composition, and activation patterns survive transection and speed changes, supporting spinal-level synergy control and grounding a pattern-formation network organization for the two-level CPG.

title: Gating and reversal of reflexes in ankle muscles during human walking
notes: In walking humans, electrical stimulation at the ankle produced phase- and intensity-dependent reflex effects: low-intensity swing-phase stimuli suppressed tibialis anterior activity, high-intensity stimuli facilitated it (largest mid-swing and correlated with exaggerated dorsiflexion), and some subjects showed a phase-dependent reversal from swing-phase tibialis anterior responses to gastrocnemius facilitation during early stance, demonstrating central gating and modulation of reflex transmission rather than simple scaling of ongoing EMG.
animal_study: Replicate the phase-dependent stimulation protocol with identified afferent stimulation in decerebrate walking cats to localize the spinal circuitry underlying the observed gating and reflex reversal.
robot_sim: Implement phase- and intensity-dependent reflex gating in a neuromechanical walker: ankle-afferent stimulation suppresses tibialis anterior in swing at low intensity, facilitates it at high intensity, and reverses to gastrocnemius facilitation in early stance; test the balance contribution during perturbations.

title: Bipedal Robots: A Systematic Review of Dynamical Models, Balance Control Strategies, and Locomotion Methods
notes: Systematic review of bipedal robotics: dynamical models from LIPM through centroidal to whole-body dynamics; balance strategies from ankle/hip to whole-body control; and locomotion methods split between model-based (ZMP, Capture Point, DCM) and learning-based (RL, human motion data), with sensor fusion, energy-aware RL rewards, and hierarchical architectures proposed as the road ahead.

title: Inter-leg coordination in the control of walking speed in Drosophila
notes: The transition from one gait to another is discontinuous and it can be shown that quadrupeds select the energetically optimal gait at a given speed (Hoyt and Taylor, 1981).

title: Initiation of locomotion in mammals.
notes: Reviews brainstem initiation of locomotion: c-fos-labeled active cells during locomotion localize the mesencephalic locomotor region across the periaqueductal gray, cuneiform nucleus, pedunculopontine nucleus, and locus coeruleus, with different subsets of locomotor nuclei apparently activated in different behavioral contexts (exploratory, appetitive, defensive), implying that lesion studies must be interpreted relative to the nuclei active in the specific locomotor task tested.
animal_study: Context-specific c-fos mapping combined with stimulation or lesions of individual mesencephalic locomotor region nuclei during exploratory versus defensive locomotion would test the context-dependent recruitment scheme.
robot_sim: Implement a supraspinal initiation module with context-selective drives (exploratory, appetitive, defensive) converging on the spinal locomotor network, mimicking the brainstem command structure; ablate submodules to mirror the lesion-study interpretation caveats.

title: Distribution of networks generating and coordinating locomotor activity in the neonatal rat spinal cord in vitro: a lesion study
notes: Lesion study in the neonatal rat spinal cord in vitro: the rhythm-generating network is distributed over the entire lumbar enlargement and extends into caudal thoracic segments (the ventral third alone suffices; sagittal lateral fragments do not), and the left–right alternation pathways run primarily in the ventral commissure.

title: Six-legged walking in insects: how CPGs, peripheral feedback, and descending signals generate coordinated and adaptive motor rhythms
notes: Reviews insect six-legged walking: how leg central pattern generators interact with sensory signals from the leg in generating single-leg stepping, how those interactions are reconfigured for forward and backward walking, curve walking, and speed changes, and how descending signals from the brain mediate initiation, maintenance, modification, and cessation of walking, with emphasis on knowledge gaps addressable by neurogenetic approaches.
animal_study: Neurogenetic silencing of identified leg sensory organs or CPG interneurons during free walking across directions and speeds in insects, targeting the intersegmental coordination gaps the review identifies.
robot_sim: Implement hexapod leg CPGs coupled to leg sensory signals with reconfigurable interactions for backward walking, curve walking, and speed changes; ablate individual sensory channels to quantify loss of motor flexibility.

title: Proprioceptive Control of Extensor Activity during Fictive Scratching and Weight Support Compared to Fictive Locomotion
notes: Shows that extensor group I afferents' oligosynaptic inhibition of extensor motoneurons at rest is replaced by oligosynaptic excitation not only during fictive locomotion but also during fictive scratching and fictive weight support, with extensor group I input affecting burst amplitude and timing similarly across tasks, evidence for state-dependent opening of excitatory group I reflex pathways during multiple motor behaviors and for a common rhythm-generating network shared by scratching and locomotion.
animal_study: Test the task-generality of the excitatory group I pathway by measuring extensor group I effects during additional motor behaviors, and dissociate the scratching and locomotion rhythms with targeted spinal lesions to test the common-network hypothesis.
robot_sim: Implement state-dependent group I extensor reflex pathways that switch from inhibitory at rest to excitatory during locomotor activity across multiple motor tasks; ablating the state switch should remove extensor load regulation during stance.

title: Depression of group Ia monosynaptic EPSPs in cat hindlimb motoneurones during fictive locomotion.
notes: During brainstem-evoked fictive locomotion in decerebrate cats, monosynaptic group Ia EPSPs are tonically depressed to about two-thirds of control in most motoneurones, with group I field potentials similarly reduced and only weak correlation with decreased motoneurone input resistance — evidence that presynaptic inhibition of Ia transmission underlies the tonic depression of stretch reflexes during locomotion.

title: Depression of muscle and cutaneous afferent-evoked monosynaptic field potentials during fictive locomotion in the cat.
notes: During MLR-evoked fictive locomotion in decerebrate cats, monosynaptic field potentials evoked by group I, group II, and cutaneous afferents are tonically depressed (intermediate-lamina group II potentials down to a mean of 49% of control), with smaller phase-dependent cyclic modulation superimposed. The depression begins with tonic MLR drive before rhythm onset, indicating that the locomotor state reduces synaptic transmission from primary afferents onto first-order spinal interneurons — afferent influx to the locomotor circuitry is gated down at its earliest synapse during locomotion.
animal_study: Replicate in mouse or rat with genetic access to interneuron classes, measuring whether afferent-evoked field-potential depression scales with locomotor drive or frequency, and separate presynaptic from postsynaptic contributors with paired-pulse and intracellular recordings across dorsal vs intermediate laminae.
robot_sim: Implement locomotor-state gating on afferent input channels: scale group I/II/cutaneous afferent synaptic gains by a tonic depression factor (~0.8 for dorsal/group I, ~0.5 for intermediate group II) plus a small phase-dependent component, and verify reflex amplitudes are suppressed during locomotion while phase-cycling as observed.

title: Pontine reticulospinal projections in the neonatal mouse: Internal organization and axon trajectories.
notes: Retrograde tracing in the neonatal mouse shows the pontine reticulospinal projection consists of segregated ipsi- and contralaterally projecting populations (3:1 ipsilateral) that are predominantly excitatory (GAD-negative) with distinct brainstem and spinal axon trajectories; the larger size and greater number of the uncrossed population accounts for its more reliable transmission to spinal motoneurons. This is the anatomical substrate for the powerful descending reticulospinal drive assumed in spinal locomotor models.

title: The flexion synergy, mother of all synergies and father of new models of gait
notes: The flexion synergy of Sherrington's flexor reflex, the withdrawal-reflex modules of Schouenborg, and the neonatal locomotor modules of Dominici largely overlap, and the end-of-stance facilitation of the flexion synergy — broadly afferent-facilitated but load-suppressed — points to a flexor burst generator as the core of an asymmetric CPG model whose afferent gating has already been implemented in walking bipedal robots.

title: A Generalized Linear Integrate-and-Fire Neural Model Produces Diverse Spiking Behaviors
notes: Computational model study. In this study, we describe a generalization of the leaky integrate-and-fire model that produces a wide variety of spiking behaviors while still being analytically solvable between firings.

title: A unified view of quiet and perturbed stance: simultaneous co-existing excitable modes
notes: Here we present evidence that a single- segment characterization of quiet stance is inadequate.

title: Load-regulating mechanisms in gait and posture: Comparative aspects.
notes: Type Ib feedback has an inhibitory effect on muscles in non-moving animals

title: Dynamic Sensorimotor Interactions in Locomotion
notes: Definitive synthesis of locomotion as a dynamic interaction between a genetically determined spinal CPG and sensory feedback: extensor proprioceptive input adjusts stance timing and amplitude to locomotor speed while being silenced in the opposite phase, and skin afferents predominantly correct limb and foot placement during stance on uneven terrain. Transmission in locomotor pathways is modulated in a state- and phase-dependent manner through shared presynaptic, interneuronal, and motoneuronal mechanisms, keeping the central program and feedback congruous.
animal_study: Phase-matched perturbation series in spinal animals (ramp loading/unloading of extensors at each cycle phase, phase-matched skin stimulation) to map the state- and phase-dependent gating the review synthesizes.
robot_sim: Build the controller as CPG plus phase-gated feedback: extensor proprioceptive channels active only during stance (silenced in swing) adjusting timing and amplitude to speed, and cutaneous placement-correction reflexes active during stance — then test gait adaptation to speed and uneven terrain.

title: Intrinsic function of a neuronal network — a vertebrate central pattern generator
notes: Computational model study. The role of different subtypes of Ca 2q channels, Ca2q dependent Kq channels and voltage dependent NMDA channels at the neuronal and network level is in focus as well as the effects of different metabotropic, aminergic and peptidergic modulators that target these ion channels.

title: Toward Mission Capable Legged Robots through Biological Inspiration
An ontogenetic model for the sensorimotor organization of balance control in humans
notes: Review of ontogenetic model sensorimotor organization. Computational model study. the basis of a review of the literature including the authors’ own experimental studies, a model for the ontogenesis of balance control in children was developed.

title: Speed-dependent turning strategies in quadrupedal locomotion: insights from computational modeling
notes: Extends the 2024 quadrupedal model with three asymmetric steering mechanisms — body bending, lateral force, and lateral limb shifting — compared across walking speeds: bending wins at low speed, lateral force at medium, lateral shifting at high, with forelimbs consistently leading steering and hindlimbs adjusting propulsion and stability per strategy.

title: Contribution of sensory feedback to ongoing ankle extensor activity during the stance phase of walking
notes: Quantitative review establishing that load-related sensory feedback contributes up to 60% of ongoing ankle extensor activity during the stance phase of walking, with secondary spindle endings (human) and Golgi tendon organs (human and cat) the likely receptors — autogenic positive feedback reinforcing stance extensor force. Argues that resolving which receptor groups set extensor magnitude across locomotor tasks requires network simulations coupled to forward-dynamic musculoskeletal models, since experimental strategies alone cannot dissociate the distributed contributions.
animal_study: Selectively block candidate receptor pathways (tendon organ vs spindle secondary) during loaded walking in cats to apportion the up-to-60% extensor enhancement between Ib and II afferents across locomotor tasks and speeds.
robot_sim: Implement autogenic positive force feedback (Ib) and length/velocity feedback (II) onto stance-gated ankle extensor motoneurons; ablate each channel in turn and test whether unloading reduces extensor activity by up to 60% as reported.

title: Five basic muscle activation patterns account for muscle activity during human locomotion
notes:
We recorded from12–16 ipsilateral leg and trunk muscles
using both surface and intramuscular recording and determined the average, normalized EMG
of each record for 10–15 consecutive step cycles. We identified five basic underlying factors or
component waveforms that can account for about 90% of the total waveform variance across
different muscles during normal gait. Furthermore, while activation patterns of individual
muscles could vary dramatically with speed and gravitational load, both the limb kinematics
and the basic EMG components displayed only limited changes. Thus, we found a systematic
phase shift of all five factors with speed in the same direction as the shift in the onset of the swing
phase. This tendency for the factors to be timed according to the lift-off event supports the idea
that the origin of the gait cycle generation is the propulsion rather than heel strike event. The
basic invariance of the factors with walking speed and with body weight unloading implies
that a few oscillating circuits drive the active muscles to produce the locomotion kinematics.
A flexible and dynamic distribution of these basic components to the muscles may result
from various descending and proprioceptive signals that depend on the kinematic and kinetic
demands of the movements

Electrophysiology of a Dendritic Neuron Model

title: Central pattern generators in the brainstem and spinal cord: an overview of basic principles, similarities and differences.
notes: Comparative overview of brainstem and spinal CPGs (deglutition, mastication, respiration, defecation, micturition, ejaculation, locomotion) showing that organization, function, and cellular properties are generally well-preserved phylogenetically across in vivo models, in vitro preparations, and primates, with the locomotor network the most fully characterized — supporting transfer of locomotor CPG design principles across species and preparations.
animal_study: Use the comparative framework: test whether a CPG motif characterized in one in vitro preparation (e.g., rhythmogenic burster types) reproduces its role when assayed in another species' spinal preparation under equivalent pharmacological activation.
robot_sim: Use the review's summary of conserved CPG organization (modular rhythmogenic units, descending trigger and steering inputs) as the architectural template for a simulated network controlling multiple rhythmic behaviors, not only locomotion.

title: Human lumbar cord circuitries can be activated by extrinsic tonic input to generate locomotor-like activity
notes:
Cited by Geyer and Herr, 2010.
We have demonstrated that non-patterned electrical stimulation of the lumbar cord can induce stepping-like activity in the lower limbs of complete spinal cord injured individuals. This result suggested the existence of a human lumbar locomotor pattern generator, which can convert a tonic input to a rhythmic motor output. We have studied the human lumbar cord in isolation from supraspinal input but under extrinsic tonic input delivered by spinal cord stimulation. Large-diameter afferents within the posterior roots are directly depolarized by the electrical stimulation. These afferents project to motoneurons as well as to lumbar interneurons involved in the motor control of lower limbs. Stimulation at 25–50Hz can elicit rhythmic alternating flexion/extension movements of the lower limbs in supine individuals. Reducing the tonic input frequency to 5–15Hz initiates lower limb extension. Epidural stimulation applied during manually assisted treadmill stepping in complete spinal cord injured persons immediately increases the central state of excitability of lumbar cord networks and enhances stepping-like functional motor outputs. Sustained, non-patterned tonic input via the posterior roots can activate human lumbar cord networks. Pattern generating configurations of these multifunctional circuitries can be set-up depending on the stimulation parameters and particularly on the input frequency.

title: Modelling spinal circuitry involved in locomotor pattern generation: insights from the effects of afferent stimulation
notes: Computational model of 2 level CPG

title: Computational modeling of spinal circuits controlling limb coordination and gaits in quadrupeds
notes: Interactions between cervical and lumbar spinal circuits are mediated by long propriospinal neurons (LPNs). Ablation of descending LPNs in mice disturbs left-right coordination at high speeds without affecting fore-hind alternation. We developed a computational model of spinal circuits consisting of four rhythm generators coupled by commissural interneurons (CINs), providing left-right interactions, and LPNs, mediating homolateral and diagonal interactions. The proposed CIN and diagonal LPN connections contribute to speed-dependent gait transition from walk, to trot, and then to gallop and bound; the homolateral LPN connections ensure fore-hind alternation in all gaits. The model reproduces speed-dependent gait expression in intact and genetically transformed mice and the disruption of hindlimb coordination following ablation of descending LPNs. Inputs to CINs and LPNs can affect interlimb coordination and change gait independent of speed. We suggest that these interneurons represent the main targets for supraspinal and sensory afferent signals adjusting gait.

title: Neural Adaptive Nonlinear MIMO Control for Bipedal Walking Robot Locomotion in Hazardous and Complex Task Applications
notes: Neural adaptive MIMO control (nonlinear dynamic inversion plus RBF networks with finite-time convergence) on a 5-DOF underactuated Rabbit biped holds stable limit cycles through +100% trunk-mass, ±30% limb-inertia, and torque-saturation perturbations, outperforming four benchmark controllers on real dSPACE hardware.

title: On the central generation of locomotion in the low spinal cat
notes:
Cited by Geyer and Herr, 2010.
Total afferent inhibition.

A central network of neurones in the spinal cord has been shown to produce a rhythmic motor output similar to locomotion after suppression of all afferent inflow. The experiments were performed mainly in acute spinal cats (th. 12), which had received DOPA i.v. and the monoamine oxidase inhibitor Nialamide. In some preparations all dorsal roots supplying the spinal cord were transected, in others phasic afferent activity was suppressed by curarization. The activity was recorded as neurograms from nerve filaments or as electromyograms.

It is concluded that:

1. alternating activity between flexors and extensors of foot, ankle, knee, and hip of one limb can still occur

2. the duration of the flexor discharges vary less with the cycle duration than the extensor discharges

3. different flexor muscles may retain individual patterns

4. the activity at different joints can be dissociated

5. there is at least one network for each limb

6. the coordination between the two hindlimbs can be alternating as in walking or be more closely spaced as in galloping

7. alternating activity in the ankle remains even when only segments L6, L7 and S1 are intact.

title: Biorobotic approaches to the study of motor systems
notes: Early position paper establishing biorobotics as a two-way interface between biology and robotics — robots as physical models of biological systems and as recipients of biological design principles — with initial progress in biorobotic studies of locomotion, orientation, and vertebrate arm control.
robot_sim: Adopt the biorobotic loop: use a legged robot or its simulation as a physical hypothesis of the biological motor system (locomotion, orientation, arm control) and feed its failure modes back to revise the underlying neural model.

title: Integration of posture and locomotion in acute decerebrate cats and in awake, freely moving cats
notes: Integration of posture and locomotion in decerebrate cats: postural set and locomotion share circuitry, with tonically controlled parallel descending systems.

title: Regulation of Arm and Leg Movement during Human Locomotion
notes: Synthesis that both arms and legs during human locomotion are regulated by central pattern generators, with sensory feedback regulating CPG activity and assisting interlimb coordination; coupling strength is stronger between the legs than between the arms, but all four limbs are similarly governed by CPG activity and reflex control.
animal_study: Perturb a single limb during locomotion (nerve stimulation or sudden loading) and measure phase-coupled reflex changes in the other three limbs to map the arm-leg versus leg-leg coupling hierarchy the review proposes.
robot_sim: Implement four limb oscillators (a quadrupedal-style CPG) with weaker arm-leg than leg-leg coupling plus afferent phase modulation of each oscillator; test whether arm-swing entrainment matches human interlimb coordination data.

title: Dual-mode operation of neuronal networks involved in left-right alternation
notes: Intersectional mouse genetics shows that ablating the V0 commissural population forces quadrupedal hopping at all locomotor frequencies, while selective ablation splits the system into dual modes: inhibitory V0 neurons are required for left-right alternation at low speeds (mixed coordination at medium, alternation at high), and excitatory V0 neurons for alternation at low speeds with hopping at medium/high speeds. Left-right coordination is thus implemented by two molecularly distinct commissural modules whose recruitment is speed-dependent — a modular logic that may constrain species-specific, frequency-dependent gait expression.
animal_study: Beyond the performed ablations, conditionally silence each V0 subgroup at defined locomotor speeds (pharmacogenetics) while recording commissural activity, to confirm the causal frequency handoff between inhibitory and excitatory left-right coupling.
robot_sim: Implement dual-mode commissural coupling in a CPG: inhibitory left-right coupling dominant at low oscillation frequency, excitatory coupling recruited at high frequency; ablate each module and verify the model reproduces the hopping versus alternation phenotypes as a function of drive.

title: Activity of interneurons mediating reciprocal 1a inhibition during locomotion
notes: The data obtained show that during locomotion there are at least two sources of inhibition of motoneurons of antagonistic muscles: (i) the activity of 1a afferents of the active muscle, mediating by corresponding interneurons; and (ii) signals coming through the same interneurons from the central mechanisms generating stepping movements.

title: Group I extensor afferents evoke disynaptic EPSPs in cat hindlimb extensor motorneurones during fictive locomotion.
notes: During the extension (stance-equivalent) phase of MLR-evoked fictive locomotion in decerebrate cats, group I afferents from ankle extensors evoke disynaptic EPSPs (mean central latency 1.55 ms, single interposed interneuron) in hip, knee, and ankle extensor motoneurons — also elicited by selective group Ia activation via muscle stretch — with hip extensor motoneurons receiving excitation from both homonymous and ankle extensor nerves. The effect arises from cyclic disinhibition of excitatory interneurons rather than motoneuronal voltage-dependent conductances or flexion-phase presynaptic inhibition: a stance-gated group I positive reflex enhancing extensor force production during stance.
animal_study: Intracellular recordings from identified extensor motoneurons across locomotor speeds and loading states to test whether the disynaptic group I excitation scales with stance load, and to localize the disinhibitory gate on the excitatory interneuron population.
robot_sim: Implement a disynaptic excitatory pathway from extensor group I afferents to extensor motoneurons, gated ON during extension via interneuron disinhibition (OFF during flexion); ablate it and test for loss of stance force reinforcement.

title: Ionic mechanisms underlying bistability in spinal motoneurons: insights from a computational model
notes: Conductance-based modeling with mouse slice recordings identifies a minimal mechanistic core for motoneuron plateau potentials and bistable firing: synergistic ICaL + CICR + ICAN interactions, promoted by persistent sodium current and opposed by Ca2+-dependent K+ current — a tractable basis for interpreting dysregulated excitability in spasticity.

title: Muscle proprioceptors in adult rat: mechanosensory signaling and synapse distribution in spinal cord
notes: In adult rats, functionally identified triceps surae proprioceptors (Ia, II, Ib) project and distribute provisional synapses in the spinal cord much as in the cat, but rat Ib afferents fire robustly during passive muscle stretch and Ia afferents show exaggerated dynamic responses even after locomotor scaling is accounted for — mechanosensory coding is species-adapted, so cat-derived afferent transfer functions cannot be transferred to other species without correction.
animal_study: Record Ia/II/Ib firing during active locomotion (not only passive stretch) in rats and another mid-size species, testing whether the species-specific dynamic gains persist in vivo and reshape reflex equilibria predicted from cat data.
robot_sim: Instantiate afferent encoders with rat-specific gains (exaggerated Ia dynamic response, stretch-sensitive Ib) rather than cat transfer functions in a rat-scale neuromuscular leg model; test controller sensitivity to the species differences.

title: Stimulus-Dependent Changes in the Vestibular Contribution to Human Postural Control
notes: Computational model study. The goal of this study was to test this sensory-reweighting hypothesis using measures that quantitatively assess the relative contributions of the proprioceptive and graviceptive (vestibular) sys- tems to postural control during eyes-closed stance in different test conditions.

title: Neuromechanical Principles Underlying Movement Modularity and Their Implications for Rehabilitation
notes:
Neuromechanical principles define the properties and problems that shape neural solutions for movement.
Although the theoretical and experimental evidence is debated, we present arguments for consistent structures in motor patterns, i.e., motor modules, that are neuromechanical solutions for movement particular
to an individual and shaped by evolutionary, developmental, and learning processes. As a consequence,
motor modules may be useful in assessing sensorimotor deficits specific to an individual and define targets
for the rational development of novel rehabilitation therapies that enhance neural plasticity and sculpt motor
recovery. We propose that motor module organization is disrupted and may be improved by therapy in spinal
cord injury, stroke, and Parkinson’s disease. Recent studies provide insights into the yet-unknown underlying neural mechanisms of motor modules, motor impairment, and motor learning and may lead to better
understanding of the causal nature of modularity and its underlying neural substrates.

title: Proprioceptive regulation of locomotion.
feedback: Ia or II stance to swing
notes: Review of proprioceptive regulation across walking systems: during locomotion, Golgi tendon organ feedback from extensor muscles reverses from inhibition to excitation, maintaining stance while the extensors are loaded and helping time the stance-to-swing transition, while primary and secondary spindle afferents also influence the timing of the rhythm — establishing phase-dependent reflex reversal as a general feature of cat and arthropod walking.

title: How swifts control their glide performance with morphing wings
notes: Computational model study. Here we describe the aerodynamic and structural performance of actual swift wings, as measured in a wind tunnel, and on this basis build a semi- empirical glide model.

title: Using animal data and neural dynamics to reverse engineer a neuromechanical rat model
Proprioceptive Feedback and Movement Regulation
notes: Comprehensive treatment of proprioceptive feedback in movement regulation spanning muscle spindle, tendon organ, joint, ligament, skin, and invertebrate proprioceptors, their firing during active movement (including task-related fusimotor set), and a control-theoretic framing: stretch reflexes as proportional control, positive force feedback via tendon organs, finite-state logic of postural constraints, and inherent feedback from muscle properties.
animal_study: Dissociate fusimotor from extrafusal drive during locomotion: record spindle Ia/II and tendon organ Ib activity while independently manipulating muscle load and length in walking animals, per the review's framework for separating receptor contributions.
robot_sim: Build the control hierarchy in simulation: proportional Ia feedback, positive Ib force feedback, finite-state (phase-gated) reflex switching, and muscle-property-mediated preflexes; ablate each layer to quantify its contribution to stable movement.

title: Activation of the central pattern generators for locomotion by serotonin and excitatory amino acids in neonatal rat.
notes: In the isolated neonatal rat brainstem–spinal cord, bath-applied serotonin (acting via 5-HT1/5-HT2, not 5-HT3 receptors) and excitatory amino acids (NMDA- and non-NMDA-receptor dependent) elicit right–left alternating fictive locomotion with dose-dependent cycle period (10→5 s for 5-HT, 3→1 s for EAA agonists) — the standard pharmacological activation assay for the mammalian locomotor CPG in vitro.

title: Patterns of locomotor drive to motoneurons and last-order interneurons: clues to the structure of the CPG.
notes: During fictive locomotion in decerebrate cats, low-threshold cutaneous reflex pathways to the flexor digitorum longus motor pool are differentially controlled at the level of last-order excitatory interneurons, and the modulation pattern is preserved whether FDL fires in early flexion or during extension. The motor pool and reflex-modulation patterns reveal distinct early versus late flexion components, and pattern formation can be separated from rhythm generation — evidence the CPG embodies partially distinct neural organizations for these two functions.
animal_study: Record from identified last-order cutaneous interneurons during normal and perturbed stepping to test whether the early/late-flexion split in reflex gating maps onto distinct interneuron populations, as the provisional circuit diagram predicts.
robot_sim: Implement a CPG with separable rhythm-generator and pattern-formation modules plus phase-gated cutaneous reflex gains following the early- versus late-flexion modulation; ablate the pattern module to test rhythm persistence with altered motoneuron scheduling.

title: Ensemble firing of muscle afferents recorded during normal locomotion in cats
notes: Chronic recordings during normal cat stepping show that ensemble spindle afferent firing is largely predictable from muscle length and velocity alone (with significant EMG-linked fusimotor action in triceps surae), and that the ensemble of triceps surae tendon organ afferents accurately encodes whole-muscle force. To a first approximation, large muscle afferents in the cat hindlimb signal muscle velocity (Ia), length (II), and force (Ib) at locomotor speeds and amplitudes.
animal_study: Repeat the ensemble afferent recording approach during perturbed and sloped walking to test the robustness of velocity/length/force encoding under altered load and fusimotor state.
robot_sim: Instantiate afferent feedback as ensemble codes (Ia proportional to muscle velocity, II to length, Ib ensemble averaging to whole-muscle force) rather than single-unit transfer functions in a locomotion controller, and verify feedback control survives realistic firing variance and fusimotor modulation.

title: Afferent-mediated modulation of the soleus muscle activity during the stance phase of human walking
notes: In human walking, slow small-amplitude ankle dorsiflexion perturbations during stance modulate ongoing soleus activity through group II afferent feedback (response reduced by tizanidine depression of group II pathways) with at least a partial group Ia contribution; blocking sensory feedback from the foot had no effect, and body-load changes shifted baseline activity without changing response amplitude. Group II and possibly load-sensitive afferents govern stance-phase extensor amplitude, whereas foot cutaneous and intrinsic proprioceptive afferents do not contribute.
animal_study: Replicate the double dissociation (tizanidine group II depression vs foot anesthesia vs load change) in cat or rodent walking to test whether group II dominance in stance extensor modulation is species-general or human-specific.
robot_sim: Implement ankle stretch-mediated group II feedback (plus partial Ia) onto stance-phase soleus/extensor motoneurons; reproduce the perturbation-response amplitude, its persistence under load change, and its reduction when group II gain is removed.

title: Strategies for dynamic stability during adaptive human locomotion
notes: Frames dynamic stability in adaptive human locomotion as an interplay among multiple balance strategies across the sudden support-surface transitions of every bipedal step, with visual, vestibular, and kinesthetic sensory information plus knowledge and prior experience all contributing to strategy selection — stability emerges from distributed, sensory-gated strategy interaction rather than a single mechanism.
animal_study: Apply phase-specific visual, vestibular, and proprioceptive perturbations during obstacle negotiation and uneven-terrain walking to map which sensory modality gates which stabilizing strategy.
robot_sim: Implement a layered balance-strategy controller (weight-shifting, stepping, arm reactions) with multimodal sensory gating in a biped simulation; ablate individual strategies to identify the minimum set required for stable adaptive walking.

title: Adaptive Control Responses to Behavioral Perturbation Based Upon the Insect
notes: Final report on Eglin AFB-supported Case Western Reserve work on decision behaviors in insect walking: quantitative descriptions of cockroaches choosing to climb over or tunnel under barriers, brain-lesion experiments localizing where descending turning commands are formulated, and a robotic leg built to test the hypotheses at the systems level.

title: Computer simulation of stepping in the hind legs of the cat: an examination of mechanisms regulating the stance-to-swing transition.
notes: A three-dimensional simulation of cat hind-leg stepping shows that stance termination governed by ankle extensor force (load) signals — alone or combined with hip position — yields stable stepping and correct interleg timing, whereas the hip position signal alone fails; mutual inhibition between controllers restores stability but not correct timing. Coordination depends critically on load-sensitive signals from each leg, with mechanical linkages mediated by these signals playing a significant role in establishing the alternating gait.
animal_study: The model's signal ranking predicts that selectively removing ankle extensor force feedback (tendon organ blockade) in walking cats destabilizes stepping more than removing hip position afferents — a direct lesion test of the stance-to-swing signal hierarchy.
robot_sim: Reproduce directly: gate the stance-to-swing transition on thresholded ankle-extensor force (with and without hip-angle gating) in a hind-leg/biped model, ablate each channel, and verify the load channel is necessary for stable alternation and correct contralateral timing.

title: Evaluation of intracellular labeling with micron-sized particles of iron oxide (MPIOs) as a general tool for in vitro and in vivo tracking of human stem and progenitor cells.
notes: Intracellular labeling with micron-sized iron oxide particles (MPIOs) gives MRI-detectable tracking of human stem and progenitor cells with superior detectability over smaller iron oxide particles, but labeling and uptake efficiencies vary strongly across the six tested human cell types, so labeling must be validated per cell type.

title: Experiments and models of sensorimotor interactions during locomotion
notes: Review establishing that cutaneous and muscle afferent input is continuously integrated with the locomotor CPG and can strongly affect the timing and amplitude of locomotor activity, with transmission gated centrally by the state of the system (rest vs locomotion) and modulated according to task phase — biologically relevant walking models must incorporate these spinal-level sensorimotor interactions into the control system rather than relying on feedforward pattern generation alone.
animal_study: Use phase- and state-matched afferent stimulation protocols in spinal animals to quantify how identical stimuli recruit different pathways at rest versus during locomotion and across cycle phases.
robot_sim: Add phase- and state-gated afferent channels to a CPG-driven musculoskeletal model (reflex gains scheduled by locomotor state and cycle phase) and demonstrate task-adaptive walking that a fixed-gain controller cannot achieve.

title: A quantitative description of membrane current and its application to conduction and excitation in nerve
notes: Title-level grounding only, because the supplied abstract is publisher boilerplate with no scientific content: this is the foundational quantitative description of membrane current and its application to conduction and excitation in nerve, i.e. the origin of conductance-based membrane modeling that later neuron-level CPG models build on. Re-fetch the true abstract before using this record for mechanism claims.

title: Optogenetic dissection reveals multiple rhythmogenic modules underlying locomotion
notes: Optogenetic activation of spinal excitatory and inhibitory populations shows that locomotor-like bursting can be induced unilaterally and independently in flexor or extensor networks, and that individual flexor motor pools can be recruited into bursting without any activity in nearby flexor pools. The mammalian locomotor CPG is therefore a distributed assembly of many intrinsically rhythmogenic modules rather than a single unitary oscillator, discriminating among several proposed architectures for rhythm generation in vertebrates.
animal_study: In an isolated spinal cord, unilaterally photo-activate or silence flexor versus extensor populations and single motor pools while recording across segments; testing whether silencing candidate modules stops rhythm in some pools but not others would establish how many independent rhythmogenic modules the network contains.
robot_sim: Build the CPG as many independently rhythmogenic modules (per side, per flexor/extensor network, even per motor pool) instead of one coupled half-center; ablating individual modules should leave the remaining modules bursting, reproducing the distributed-organization evidence.

title: Taking the Human Out of the Loop: A Review of Bayesian Optimization
notes: Review of taking human out loop:. These parameters are often specified and hard-coded into the software by various developers or teams.

title: Peripheral control of the cat's step cycle. II. Entrainment of the central pattern generators for locomotion by sinusoidal hip movements during "fictive locomotion."
notes: In low-spinal curarized cats with pharmacologically evoked fictive locomotion, sinusoidal hip movements entrain the burst pattern in strict 1:1 coordination over roughly ±5–70% of the resting burst period, with flexion-phase movements driving flexor efferents and extension driving extensors — direct evidence that hip-joint afferent feedback can pace the spinal locomotor CPG.

title: Lateral Stepping for Postural Correction in Parkinson’s Disease
notes: The objective of this study is to characterize, for the first time, the lateral stepping strategies for postural correction in patients with Parkinson’s Disease (PD) and the effect of their antiparkinson medication.

title: Epidural spinal cord stimulation as an intervention for motor recovery after motor complete spinal cord injury.
notes: Review arguing that lumbosacral epidural stimulation after motor-complete SCI acts by first depolarizing large-diameter dorsal-root proprioceptive afferents, which — integrated with interneuronal and latent residual supraspinal translesional connections — recruit locomotor centers and augment downstream motor units, with different stimulation parameters able to facilitate standing versus stepping.
animal_study: In spinal-transected animals, selectively block or lesion specific large-diameter dorsal-root afferent groups during epidural stimulation while recording locomotor-center recruitment, to identify which afferent classes are necessary for the standing-versus-stepping parameter effects.
robot_sim: Model epidural stimulation as tonic depolarization of large-diameter proprioceptive afferent inputs to the spinal network; simulate parameter-dependent switching between standing and stepping attractors to test how afferent recruitment gates locomotor centers.

title: A Neuromechanical Rat Model with a Complete Set of Hind Limb Muscles
Candidate interneurones mediating group I disynaptic EPSPs in extensor motoneurones during fictive locomotion in the cat.
notes: Identifies a candidate population of excitatory interneurons in intermediate laminae of mid-to-caudal L7 that are activated by extensor group I afferents at monosynaptic latency specifically during the extensor phase of MLR-evoked fictive locomotion, project to extensor motor nuclei, and burst rhythmically in extension even without afferent stimulation — a previously unknown population that could mediate the group I disynaptic excitation of extensor motoneurones while also supplying central extensor drive.
animal_study: Silence or lesion the candidate L7 interneurons during fictive locomotion while stimulating extensor group I afferents, to test whether they are necessary for the stance-phase disynaptic excitation of extensor motoneurones; intracellular recording would confirm the disynaptic linkage.
robot_sim: Implement stance-gated group I afferent excitation of extensor motoneurones through a disynaptic interneuron layer whose cells also carry central extensor drive; ablating either the afferent gate or the interneuron population should remove load-dependent extensor reinforcement.

title: Major role for sensory feedback in soleus EMG activity in the stance phase of walking in man.
notes: Unloading the ankle extensors for 210 ms during stance reduces soleus EMG by about 50% (64 ms onset) in human walking; the suppression survives common peroneal nerve block, excluding peripherally mediated reciprocal inhibition from antagonists, and survives ischaemia that abolishes the Ia short-latency stretch reflex, excluding group Ia. Group II and/or group Ib afferents from ankle extensors therefore carry a major part of stance-phase extensor activation in humans.
animal_study: Applying the same rapid ankle-extensor unloading paradigm in walking cats with intracellular recordings and selective group Ia/Ib/II blocks would resolve which afferent group mediates the load-dependent stance-phase excitation that human EMG cannot dissociate.
robot_sim: Implement a load-dependent extensor excitation pathway (Ib/II-analog positive force feedback) supplying a large fraction of stance-phase extensor drive; a sudden unloading event should cut extensor activity by about half within roughly 60 ms, and removing the Ia stretch reflex should leave that response intact.

title: A model of scale effects in mammalian quadrupedal running
The Effect of DOPA on the Spinal Cord 5. Reciprocal organization of pathways transmitting excitatory action to alpha motoneurones of flexors and extensors
notes: DOPA evokes a reciprocal organization of excitatory pathways to flexor and extensor alpha motoneurones — the pharmacological foundation of the half-center model of fictive locomotion.

title: Modelling genetic reorganization in the mouse spinal cord affecting left–right coordination during locomotion
notes: A computational model of the left-right commissural circuitry (inhibitory and excitatory commissural interneuron populations plus an EphA4-positive subpopulation) reproduces the gait phenotypes of axon-guidance mutations — EphA4 knockout converts to synchronized hopping via crossed excitation, Netrin-1 knockout by loss of contralateral inhibition, DCC knockout by loss of both — and shows amplified inhibition restores alternation in EphA4 and DCC knockouts but not Netrin-1 knockouts.

title: A graphics-based software system to develop and analyze models of musculoskeletal structures
notes: Computational model study. -We have created a graphics-based software system that enables users to develop and analyze musculoskeletal models without programming.

title: Biological Pattern Generation: The Cellular and Computational Logic of Networks in Motion
notes: Review articulating the 'circuit doctrine' for motor pattern generation: the mode of operation of central motor-program (CPG) networks, the neural mechanisms by which they are selected and activated for behavior, and the utility of computational models in analyzing the dynamic actions of these motor networks.
animal_study: Experiments identifying the signals that select and activate pattern-generator networks for different motor tasks in intact animals (for example recordings during task switching) directly address the review's central question about activation and selection logic.
robot_sim: Build computational models of motor networks whose operating points and activation can be manipulated, using them as the analysis tool the review prescribes for dissecting the dynamics of CPG circuits.

title: Central control of interlimb coordination and speed-dependent gait expression in quadrupeds.
notes: Computational demonstration that one spinal circuit with commissural and intralimb coupling reorganizes across speeds to express walk, trot, and gallop — gait expression emerges from speed-dependent coordination, not separate CPGs.

title: Models of ensemble firing of muscle spindle afferents recorded during normal locomotion in cats
notes: Mathematical models of muscle spindle primary (presumed Ia) firing, validated against chronically recorded hamstring afferents over 132 cat step cycles, are dominated by muscle velocity — firing rate scales approximately with the square root of velocity (power-law exponents 0.5-0.6) — with only small EMG-linked fusimotor components; inverse models recover muscle length accurately from firing profiles, implying the CNS could decode muscle length simply from Ia ensemble firing.
animal_study: Chronically record spindle Ia afferents from muscles strongly recruited in stepping to test whether velocity-dominant encoding with modest fusimotor scaling generalizes beyond hamstrings, and compare ramp-and-hold versus step-cycle responses to probe the proposed attenuation of length sensitivity at high velocities.
robot_sim: Use a square-root-of-velocity-dominant spindle encoder with a small EMG-linked fusimotor term as the Ia block in reflex models, and run it in reverse to estimate muscle length from afferent firing for state estimation in a neurally controlled walker.

title: Central Pattern Generator for Locomotion: Anatomical, Physiological, and Pathophysiological Considerations
notes: Century-spanning review concluding that walking, flying, and swimming are largely controlled by spinal central pattern generator networks, demonstrated across vertebrate species from lamprey to human, which can self-produce basic rhythmic coordinated movements even in the absence of descending or peripheral inputs; CPG plasticity is then linked to Restless Legs Syndrome, Periodic Leg Movement, Alternating Leg Muscle Activation, and Uner Tan Syndrome.
animal_study: Animal models of the reviewed movement disorders could test whether plasticity of CPG elements causes the pathological rhythmic movements, for example by measuring spinal CPG excitability in lesioned animals expressing spontaneous locomotor-like activity.
robot_sim: Model excitability or plasticity changes in CPG elements and test whether they generate spontaneous locomotor-like bursts resembling the reviewed disorders, identifying which parameter changes reproduce each pathology.

title: Optimal sensorimotor transformations for balance
notes: Computational model study. Optimal sensorimotor transformations for balance Daniel B Lockhart 1 & Lena H Ting 2 Here we have identiﬁed a sensorimotor transformation that is used by a mammalian nervous system to produce a multijoint motor behavior.

title: A Survey on CPG-Inspired Control Models and System Implementation
notes: Survey of two decades of CPG-inspired robot locomotion control across abstraction levels: CPGs modeled as coupled neuron groups generate rhythmic signals without sensory feedback but require sensory feedback to shape those signals; reviews the relative advantages of the models, the main design, optimization, and implementation issues, and trends for multi-DOF articulated control.
robot_sim: Use as a comparative menu of CPG abstractions for a simulated walker: implement several abstraction levels on a common plant and evaluate the survey's design criteria (ease of design, optimization, implementation) alongside sensory-shaping variants.

title: Control of locomotor cycle durations.
notes: In MLR-evoked fictive locomotion in cats, spontaneous cycle-duration variation is carried more often by flexor than extensor phase durations (22 of 31 experiments), so the CPG is not inherently extensor- or flexor-biased; a half-center model with two parameters per timing element — background drive ('bias') and sensitivity ('gain') — fits the phase-duration plots, background drive determines which half-center is 'dominant', and normal-cat data are fitted equally well, implying sensory input and central drive combine to set locomotor phase durations.
animal_study: Manipulate background drive to each half-center (biased MLR stimulation or drug microperfusion) while measuring phase durations to test the bias/gain model's prediction of which phase becomes dominant; deafferentation separates the central from the sensory contribution.
robot_sim: Implement a half-center oscillator with independent bias and gain on each timing element; reproduce the phase-duration scaling and switch the dominant phase by redistributing background drive — a direct mechanism for duty-factor control in CPG walkers.

title: Contribution of Afferent Feedback to Adaptive Hindlimb Walking in Cats: A Neuromusculoskeletal Modeling Study
notes: A cat hindlimb neuromusculoskeletal model coupled to a half-center CPG reproduces normal walking and the adaptive movement changes when the foot steps into a hole; dynamical-systems and nullcline analysis of the coupled CPG-musculoskeleton-environment loop shows how afferent feedback mediates adaptive locomotion in ways that immobilized fictive preparations cannot reveal.
animal_study: Validate the model's afferent-dependence predictions against the original hole-stepping experiments in walking cats, with selective deafferentation or matched perturbations identifying which feedback channels the adaptation actually requires.
robot_sim: Reproduce the architecture — half-center CPG coupled to a cat hindlimb musculoskeletal model with limb afferent feedback — and ablate each afferent channel during hole-step perturbations to map which feedback is necessary for the adaptive response.

title: Position dependence of ankle joint dynamics—I. Passive mechanics
notes: These results show that large variations in joint mechanics are possible even in the absence of voluntary muscle contraction.

title: Effect of stimulating the lumbar skin caudal to a complete spinal cord injury on hindlimb locomotion
notes: Mechanical stimulation of the lumbar skin above a complete spinal transection disrupts spinal locomotion in walking cats — pinching stops stepping and abolishes weight support, focal clip stimulation reduces flexor and extensor activity and shifts paw placement caudally, with strongest effects from L3-L5 — showing cutaneous input modulates the excitability of the spinal rhythm-generating segments themselves.

title: Neuromuscular responses to gait perturbations in freely moving cats.
notes: Impeding the forward swing of a cat's foot evokes rapid elevating reactions whose mechanically elicited EMG sequences are more complex and longer lasting than electrically elicited ones; anesthetizing the foot dorsum abolishes ankle-extensor and knee-flexor responses and reduces ankle-flexor responses to simple stretch reflexes — evidence for cutaneous mediation of the placing-like reaction during stepping, with points of difference from chronic spinal kittens that challenge a purely spinal account.
animal_study: The study is itself the animal experiment; follow-ons include recording dorsal-foot cutaneous afferents and ventral-horn responses during mechanically impeded swing, and spinalization in adults versus kittens to adjudicate spinal versus supraspinal mediation.
robot_sim: Implement a swing-phase obstacle-contact reflex: a foot-dorsum cutaneous-analog sensor triggers a phased flexor activation sequence to elevate the limb over the obstacle; ablating the sensor should abolish the elevating strategy, matching the anesthesia result.

title: Mechanical aspects of legged locomotion control
notes: Review enlisting neurophysiology, biomechanics, control engineering, and nonlinear dynamics to explain effective locomotion as the integration of muscular, skeletal, and neural mechanics, using rapid arthropod terrestrial locomotion as the data-rich model system; the outlined control hypotheses and their mathematical underpinnings inspired the design of the hexapedal robot RHex.
animal_study: Each outlined control hypothesis can be probed by perturbation experiments in running arthropods (loading changes, substrate variation, obstacles) that partition the neural versus mechanical contribution to stability and maneuvering.
robot_sim: Implement the neuromechanical hypotheses in a RHex-style hexapedal simulation with compliant legs, then ablate mechanical (compliance, damping) versus neural (feedback gain) elements to quantify each hypothesis's contribution to stable rapid locomotion.

title: Functional Neuroanatomy for Posture and Gait Control
notes: Copyright © 2017 The Korean Movement Disorder Society 1 Functional Neuroanatomy for Posture and Gait Control Kaoru Takakusaki The Research Center for Brain Function and Medical Engineering, Asahikawa Medical University, Asahikawa, Japan Received: December 13, 2016 Accepted: December 15, 2016 Corresponding author: Kaoru Takakusaki, MD,...

title: Evidence for a Spinal Central Pattern Generator in Humansa
notes: Non-patterned epidural stimulation of the posterior lumbar cord (25-60 Hz, 5-9 V over L2) in complete paraplegics induces patterned, locomotor-like EMG with rhythmic alternating stance and swing — evidence that human spinal circuitry isolated from the brain can generate locomotor-like activity when externally controlled sustained stimulation replaces the tonic drive normally generated by the brain.
animal_study: In spinal-lesioned animal models, apply the same non-patterned epidural trains with selective dorsal-root blocks or rhizotomies to determine whether stimulation of the posterior structures recruits afferent fibers, and map the parameter windows that bias stance versus swing.
robot_sim: Model an externally driven spinal network: replace tonic descending drive with sustained periodic drive to an otherwise quiescent CPG and test whether alternating stance/swing output emerges with the observed stimulation-frequency dependence.

title: Neuromuscular Models for Locomotion
Do Pacemakers Drive the Central Pattern Generator for Locomotion in Mammals?
notes: Reviews mammalian locomotor rhythmogenesis and advances the working hypothesis that pacemaker neurons with intrinsic oscillatory properties are functionally integrated into the locomotor network, complementing network-based bursting as a substrate for rhythm generation in mammals.
animal_study: Identify intrinsically oscillatory spinal neurons in a mammalian fictive-locomotion preparation and selectively silence them pharmacologically or genetically to test whether the network-generated rhythm persists without pacemaker input.
robot_sim: Build a hybrid rhythm generator combining half-center network oscillation with an intrinsic pacemaker population and ablate the pacemakers to quantify changes in rhythm robustness, phase, and frequency.

title: Force Sensors in Hexapod Locomotion
feedback: trochanteral campaniform sensilla load signals to adjust MN magnitude
notes: Finite-element modeling of the cockroach leg shows that loads are sensed by leg force sensors located close to the body, where specific force vectors (body load versus propulsion) can be discriminated, and that this information is used in positive load feedback to regulate walking — design principles directly transferable to force-controlled legged robots.

title: Novel Locomotion via Biological Inspiration
notes: Robotics review translating biological design principles into machines: cockroach-tarsus-inspired passive foot compliance robustifies climbing adhesion and permits large steps and stationary turns, insect-inspired wheel-legs passively change gait on irregular terrain, and earthworm-style peristalsis drives scalable soft robots - passive mechanics can substitute for active control.
robot_sim: Implement tarsus-inspired passive foot compliance and hub-integrated passive gait-change mechanisms in a simulated hexapod or wheel-legged robot and test whether stepping robustness on irregular terrain is maintained without active control.

title: Spinal interneuronal networks in the cat: elementary components.
notes: Establishes that feline commissural interneuron networks operate as elementary building blocks incorporated into larger networks: they receive mono- and disynaptic reticulospinal and vestibulospinal input plus mono- to oligosynaptic muscle-afferent input, and reach motoneurons mono- or disynaptically, so one population can serve reflex, postural, locomotor, and voluntary coordination.
animal_study: Selectively lesion or silence identified commissural interneuron populations and test which coordinated functions - reflex, postural, locomotor, voluntary - degrade, probing the building-block organization.
robot_sim: Model left-right coordination as commissural interneuron blocks receiving mono-/disynaptic descending and muscle-afferent input; ablate individual blocks to predict which interlimb coordination components fail during walking.

title: Ratio of Shear to Load Ground-Reaction Force May Underlie the Directional Tuning of the Automatic Postural Response to Rotation and Translation
notes: This study sought to identify the sensory signals that encode perturbation direction rapidly enough to shape the directional tuning of the automatic postural response.

title: Reflexes induced by nerve stimulation in walking cats with implanted cuff electrodes.
notes: In walking cats, low-threshold cutaneous nerve input powerfully modulates the step cycle: posterior tibial stimulation just before ankle-extensor EMG onset prolongs ipsilateral flexion and contralateral extension, sural and peroneal stimulation activates ankle extensors, and identical gastrocnemius-soleus muscle-nerve stimulation has no effect - the reflexes are cutaneously mediated and phase-dependent.
animal_study: Replicate with selective afferent blockade: silence cutaneous afferents during nerve-cuff stimulation trials to confirm loss of the flexion-prolongation and extensor-activation effects, and map the effects across all step phases.
robot_sim: Implement phase-gated cutaneous reflex channels - pre-extensor-onset flexion prolongation, sural/peroneal-type extensor activation, and stance yielding - in a walking model and ablate them to test perturbation recovery.

title: Stiffness and Damping in Postural Control Increase with Age
notes: Computational model study. We investigated the effect of aging on standing balance by fitting body sway data to a previously-developed postural control model that includes active and passive stiffness and damping parameters.

title: Ankle extensor group I afferents excite extensors throughout the hindlimb during fictive locomotion in the cat.
notes: 1. The effects of stimulating hindlimb extensor nerves (100-200 ms trains, 100 Hz, < or = 2 times threshold) during the flexor and extensor phases of the locomotor step cycle were analysed in the decerebrate, paralysed cat during fictive locomotion evoked by stimulation of the mesencephalic locomotor region. 2. Stimulation during extension of either the medial gastrocnemius (MG), lateral gastrocnemius-soleus (LGS) or plantaris (Pl) nerves was equally effective in increasing the duration and amplitude of electroneurogram (ENG) activity recorded in ipsilateral ankle, knee and hip extensor nerves. Enhancement of extensor ENG activity could be evoked with near threshold stimulation intensity and appeared within 10-40 ms of the onset of ankle extensor nerve stimulation. Stimulation of anterior biceps during extension occasionally evoked a modest increase in the duration of activity of hip, knee and ankle extensors. Stimulation of quadriceps during extension enhanced the activity of proximal extensors and soleus, but inhibited other ankle extensors. 3. Selective activation of ankle extensor Ia spindle afferents by muscle stretch also enhanced ipsilateral extension. It is argued that both muscle spindle and tendon organ afferents can contribute to the increase in extensor nerve activity evoked by group I stimulation intensity during fictive locomotion. 4.
