title: Locomotor Rhythm Generation Linked to the Output of Spinal Shox2 Excitatory Interneurons
notes: Identifies Shox2 excitatory interneurons as part of the rhythm-generating kernel in the mouse spinal cord: optogenetic silencing or blocking their synaptic output perturbs locomotor rhythm without affecting left-right and flexor-extensor patterning (while ablating the Shox2 subset coinciding with V2a interneurons has no effect), and rhythmically active Shox2 cells contact other Shox2 cells, commissural neurons, and motor neurons with a preference for flexor motor pools.
animal_study: Test whether sensory afferent input accesses the Shox2 rhythm kernel - pair phase-resetting afferent stimulation with Shox2 activity monitoring, or silence Shox2 during perturbed locomotion to separate rhythm from pattern contributions.
robot_sim: Structure the CPG with a separable rhythm kernel (interconnected excitatory units biased to flexor MNs) distinct from the pattern layer; ablating the kernel in simulation should reproduce rhythm loss with preserved patterning.

title: Implications of Positive Feedback in the Control of Movement
notes: Argues with analytic neuromuscular models that tendon-organ afferents switch from negative force feedback in static posture to positive force feedback in locomotion, and that positive force feedback is stable and effective because muscle length-tension properties provide automatic gain control - stability is further supported by concomitant negative displacement feedback and, unexpectedly, by delays in the positive feedback pathway - making positive force feedback a load-compensation mechanism complementing negative displacement and velocity feedback.
animal_study: Measure the sign of autogenic force feedback in the same muscle across quiet standing and treadmill locomotion in a decerebrate cat preparation to test the posture-to-locomotion switch directly.
robot_sim: Implement stance-phase positive autogenic force feedback (Ib excitatory) on extensors with length-tension automatic gain control plus negative displacement feedback; demonstrate stability at strong gains and with realistic delays, then remove the gain control to show instability.

title: Vertebrate Pattern Generation: Overview
Neonatal Rat Spinal Cord Bulbospinal Activation of Locomotion in the In Vitro Contribution of Commissural Projections to
notes: Neonatal rat in vitro preparation in which bulbospinal activation evokes locomotion; commissural projections contribute to bilateral activation — a tractable model for descending-initiated locomotion.

title: A neural network with central pattern generators entrained by sensory feedback controls walking of a bipedal model
notes: A planar bipedal musculoskeletal model controlled by a two-level dynamic neural network — separate rhythm generator and pattern formation layers entrained by force and movement sensory feedback — walks stably without inertial sensors, a centralized posture controller, or high-level intervention, over unknown steps and slopes, demonstrating that sensory-entrained CPGs plus biomechanics suffice for robust gait.

title: Linking spinal circuit reorganization to recovery after thoracic spinal cord injury
notes: Adapting computational speed-dependent gait circuitry models to the rat reproduces both intact gait and post-injury gait after lateral hemisection versus midline contusion, revealing two injury-specific recovery routes (restored descending drive and long propriospinal detours after hemisection; sublesional reorganization after contusion), with sensitivity analysis identifying re-engaged lumbar rhythm generators and balanced lumbar commissural connectivity as the common determinants of recovered gait.
animal_study: Test the injury-specific recovery routes in rats: after lateral hemisection, block new propriospinal detour growth and assay gait; after contusion, pharmacologically silence sublesional lumbar circuits and measure whether recovered gait degrades, verifying the two routes and the shared lumbar-rhythm determinant.
robot_sim: Implement the speed-dependent gait circuitry and simulate hemisection (unilateral removal of descending drive and long propriospinal inputs) versus contusion (diffuse weakening); test which parameter restorations recover the observed gait, and run the sensitivity analysis on lumbar commissural balance.

title: Decoding the organization of spinal circuits that control locomotion
feedback: Ia or II stance to swing
notes:
Review paper.
Abstract | Unravelling the functional operation of neuronal networks and linking cellular activity
to specific behavioural outcomes are among the biggest challenges in neuroscience. In this
broad field of research, substantial progress has been made in studies of the spinal networks
that control locomotion. Through united efforts using electrophysiological and molecular
genetic network approaches and behavioural studies in phylogenetically diverse experimental
models, the organization of locomotor networks has begun to be decoded. The emergent themes
from this research are that the locomotor networks have a modular organization with distinct
transmitter and molecular codes and that their organization is reconfigured with changes to the
speed of locomotion or changes in gait.

title: Intracellular analysis of reflex pathways underlying the stumbling corrective reaction during fictive locomotion in the cat.
notes: Intracellular recordings in decerebrate cats during fictive locomotion show the stumbling corrective reaction is built from di- and trisynaptic cutaneous excitation of knee-flexor and ankle-extensor motoneurons, with locomotor-phase-dependent reconfiguration of inhibition (increased onto ankle flexors, suppressed onto extensors) and motoneuron membrane potential sculpting whether short-latency EPSPs actually recruit firing.
animal_study: Extend to intact locomotion: record intracellularly from identified knee-flexor and ankle-extensor motoneurons during real overground stumbling corrections, or selectively lesion the di-/trisynaptic cutaneous pathways to test their necessity for obstacle avoidance during swing.
robot_sim: Implement phase-gated cutaneous reflex pathways: di-/trisynaptic excitation of knee flexors and ankle extensors with reciprocal inhibitory gating (suppressed onto extensors, increased onto flexors during flexion) plus motoneuron membrane-potential sculpting, and test foot-dorsum contact responses during swing.

title: Design process and tools for dynamic neuromechanical models and robot controllers
notes: Provides a serial design pipeline for neuro-mechanical controllers: classical control methods size reflex feedback parameters, bifurcation and phase-response analysis selects CPG parameters whose oscillations entrain rapidly to sensory feedback, and batched simulation scans parameter sensitivity, a repeatable recipe for tuning controllers built from persistent-sodium-channel CPGs rhythmically inhibiting velocity-command motoneurons.
robot_sim: Directly applicable: build per-joint persistent-sodium CPGs inhibiting velocity-command motoneurons, size feedback synapses with classical control methods, pick CPG parameters from bifurcation diagrams and phase response curves so the rhythm entrains to sensory feedback, and batch-sweep parameters for sensitivity.

title: A Neural Basis for Motor Primitives in the Spinal Cord
notes: Identifies a neural substrate for motor primitives: in spinalized frogs, intermediate-zone interneurons with short-latency postspike facilitation of multiple motor pools have facilitation patterns that match the weighting vectors of statistically extracted primitives, implying dedicated interneuron sets organize individual primitives.
animal_study: Causally test the primitive-interneuron mapping: silence the specific intermediate-zone interneuron sets whose postspike facilitation matches a given primitive and measure whether that primitive drops out of evoked motor responses while the others persist.
robot_sim: Represent each motor primitive as a dedicated interneuron population with fixed postspike facilitation weights onto its motor pools; ablate individual populations to predict loss of the matching synergy component in evoked motor patterns.

title: Circuits for Grasping: Spinal dI3 Interneurons Mediate Cutaneous Control of Motor Behavior
notes: Defines the spinal microcircuit for cutaneous grip control: dI3 interneurons (marked by Isl1) relay low-threshold cutaneous afferent input to motoneurons, and genetic silencing of their output specifically abolishes the ability to scale grip force with increasing load while sparing other motor tasks.
animal_study: Determine which cutaneous afferent classes drive the dI3 grip circuit by recording dI3 responses to defined afferent stimulation, and test whether dI3 silencing similarly disrupts other cutaneously guided behaviors such as limb placement reactions during locomotion.
robot_sim: Add a dI3-analog relay layer between low-threshold tactile sensors and grip motoneurons; ablate it to reproduce the failure to scale grip force with load while other behaviors persist, a minimal circuit for tactile grip control in prosthetic or robotic hands.

title: A three-dimensional musculoskeletal model of the dog
notes: A detailed, scalable 3D dog musculoskeletal model (84 degrees of freedom, 134 muscles) whose inverse-dynamics and static-optimization pipeline recovers the three forelimb synergy groups of a walking beagle with good activation agreement, providing a simulation base for studying joint loading and neuromuscular control in quadruped locomotion.
animal_study: Use the model's predicted forelimb activations and joint loads to design targeted in-vivo measurements in dogs, e.g. instrumented implant or deep-muscle EMG validation during walk, and extend the synergy validation to other gaits and body sizes.
robot_sim: Use the 84-DOF, 134-muscle dog model as a simulation plant; replicate the inverse-dynamics, static-optimization, and hierarchical-clustering synergy pipeline, then test neural locomotion controllers against the three extracted forelimb synergies.

title: Spinal pattern generation
notes: Review framing spinal pattern generation around three foci: transmitter actions on rhythms in reduced preparations, activity-dependent changes in membrane properties of the generating circuits, and CPG-afferent interactions, emphasizing that new reflex responses and membrane properties emerge only during rhythmic activity.
animal_study: Test state-dependent reflex modulation directly: compare the same afferent stimulation in quiescent versus rhythmically active reduced preparations (neonatal rat, lamprey) to confirm that new reflex responses appear only during ongoing rhythm, as the review proposes.
robot_sim: Implement CPG circuits whose reflex pathway gains and signs are gated by rhythmic state, and test whether reflex responses absent in quiescent simulation appear when the CPG is active, mirroring state-dependent reflex modification.

title: Stumbling corrective reaction: a phase-dependent compensatory reaction during locomotion
notes: The classic characterization of the stumbling corrective reaction: dorsum contact during swing evokes short-latency flexor activation lifting the paw over the obstacle via early (~10 ms) and late (~25 ms) pathways to knee flexors, whereas the same stimulus during support inhibits-then-excites extensors and boosts the next swing's flexion, phase-dependent reflex gating organized by the spinal locomotor generator, with painful input instead evoking withdrawal throughout the cycle.
animal_study: Identify the spinal interneurons mediating the early and late knee-flexor pathways by recording during locomotion with paw-dorsum stimulation, test their necessity by lesioning them, and verify the phase-reversal rules across speeds and after spinalization.
robot_sim: Implement a phase-switched stumble reflex: paw-dorsum tactile input drives short-latency flexor bursts during swing for obstacle clearance and stance-phase extensor modulation with enhanced next-swing flexion; ablate the reflex to quantify its contribution to fall avoidance.

title: Vestibulospinal, reticulospinal and descending propriospinal nerve fibres in man
notes:
The course and location of vestibulospinal, reticulospinal
and descending propriospinal fibres in man are reported.

There is an extensive propriospinal network of reciprocal excitatory and inhibitory connections active during locomotion that may activate MNs far from the site of pattern generator

title: Goal-Directed CPG-Based Control for Tensegrity Spines with Many Degrees of Freedom Traversing Irregular Terrain
notes: Demonstrates a CPG-controlled tensegrity-spine robot with six-degree-of-freedom compliant intervertebral coupling whose neural-network-processed proprioceptive feedback and goal-directed input achieve terrain-transitioning locomotion, combining local reflexes with structural compliance to replace rigid-body control on many-DOF compliant bodies.
robot_sim: Reproduce the CPG-plus-compliant-body controller: neural-network-processed proprioceptive feedback and goal-directed input driving a tensegrity spine; ablate the feedback and the compliance separately to attribute terrain-robustness contributions.

title: Capturability-based analysis and control of legged locomotion, Part 1: Theory and application to three simple gait models
notes: Formalizes N-step capturability, the ability of a legged system to stop without falling within N steps, as a stability criterion for legged locomotion, and shows across three 3D linear-inverted-pendulum models how finite-sized feet and centroidal angular momentum (a reaction mass) each enlarge the set of capturable states relative to point-foot step placement.
robot_sim: Compute N-step capturability margins for a biped from its state and step-placement options; compare point-foot, finite-foot, and angular-momentum reaction-mass variants to quantify how each mechanism enlarges the capturable region, then use capturability as the step-selection criterion.

title: Bio-inspired controller achieving forward speed modulation with a 3D bipedal walker
notes:
In the present contribution, we embrace the idea of combining a CPG and reflexes in a neuromuscular torquebased controller for bipedal locomotion. More precisely, we design a controller capable of generating robust and humanlike locomotion gaits on a 3D bipedal walker.

In this paper, we have developed a bio-inspired torque-based controller supporting the emergence of a new generation of robust and energy-efficient walkers. It recruits virtual muscles driven by reflexes and a central pattern generator, and thus requires no computationally intensive inverse kinematics or dynamics modeling. This controller is capable of generating energyefficient and human-like gaits (both regarding kinematics and dynamics) across a large range of forward speeds, in a 3D environment. After a single off-line optimization process, the forward speed can be continuously commanded within this range by changing high-level parameters, as linear or quadratic functions of the target speed. Sharp speed transitions can then be achieved with no additional tuning, resulting in immediate adaptations of the step length and frequency. In this paper, we particularly embodied this controller on a simulated version of COMAN, a 95 cm tall humanoid robot. We reached forward speed modulations between 0.4 and 0.9 m/s. This covers normal human walking speeds once scaled to the robot size. Finally, the walker demonstrated significant robustness against a large spectrum of unpredicted perturbations: facing external push

title: Pattern generation for stick insect walking movements-multisensory control of a locomotor program
A multisensory integration model of human stance control
notes: Computational model study. We aim to apply the model in (1) the design and development of prostheses and orthoses and (2) the diagnosis of neurological balance disorders.

title: Gust Mitigation of Micro Air Vehicles Using Passive Articulated Wings
notes: A flight-validated 8-degree-of-freedom model of articulated micro air vehicles shows passive wing articulation increases gust robustness within an intermediate compliance range but degrades it when joints are too compliant, an airborne demonstration that preflexive, structure-mediated compliance robustifies locomotion only in a bounded regime.
animal_study: Test the passive-compliance robustness hypothesis on flying insects: measure natural wing-joint compliance and wing deformation under controlled gust exposure and determine whether biological compliance sits in the range where articulation improves disturbance rejection.
robot_sim: Model passive articulated joints with tunable compliance on a body subject to gust-like disturbances; identify the compliance range that maximizes disturbance rejection and verify that performance degrades when joints are made too compliant.

title: The effect of dorsal root transection on the efferent motor pattern in the cat's hindlimb during locomotion.
notes: After transecting all dorsal roots from one hindlimb, mesencephalic walking cats retain the limb's complex motor pattern, including the double-burst knee flexors and appropriately timed toe dorsiflexor, although with greater variability and occasional breakdown, showing the central network generates the full pattern without phasic afferent input while afferents stabilize and fine-tune it.
animal_study: Identify which afferent signals restore the lost reliability: selectively re-stimulate individual afferent classes in the deafferented limb during locomotion to see which feedback reduces pattern variability and prevents breakdown, mapping stabilizing versus pattern-constructing roles.
robot_sim: Ablate all sensory feedback channels in a CPG walker and test whether the joint-specific burst structure (double-burst flexors) persists with increased variability, a lesion test separating central pattern generation from afferent stabilization.

title: Stimulation of a Restricted Region in the Midline Cerebellar White Matter Evokes Coordinated Quadrupedal Locomotion in the Decerebrate Cat
notes: Identifies a cerebellar locomotor region in the midline white matter (hook bundle of Russell, crossed fastigiofugal fibers) whose low-threshold microstimulation evokes well-coordinated quadrupedal locomotion in decerebrate cats; it summates with subthreshold mesencephalic locomotor region stimulation and remains effective after MLR lesions, establishing the fastigial nucleus as an independent supraspinal site that triggers both brainstem and spinal locomotor subprograms.
animal_study: Record fastigial nucleus activity during spontaneous overground locomotion to confirm the cerebellar locomotor region is naturally engaged, and test the effects of CLR lesions on spontaneous and MLR-evoked locomotion in otherwise intact animals.
robot_sim: Implement two independent supraspinal drive sites (fastigial/CLR-analog and MLR-analog) converging on the spinal CPG with subthreshold summation; ablate each to test whether the other alone sustains locomotion, and test cycle-time shortening under combined suprathreshold drive.

title: The intrinsic factors in the act of progression in the mammal
notes: Rhythmic stepping persists in the low-spinal cat after complete deafferentation of the hindlimb muscles, and Graham Brown concluded the cycle is generated by paired antagonistic spinal centres whose balance sways through fatigue and rebound — the origin of the half-center concept — with proprioceptive input playing a regulative, not causative, role in grading steps to the terrain.

title: Muscle proprioceptive feedback and spinal networks
notes: Review assigning computational roles to segmental muscle spindle, Golgi tendon organ, and Renshaw cell feedback: generation of anti-gravity thrust during stance, locomotor phase timing, linearization of muscle nonlinearities, lever-arm and fatigue compensation, synergy formation, and selection of perturbation responses, a functional catalog of what spinal feedback contributes to motor control.
animal_study: Test individual functional roles by selective silencing: block spindle or tendon-organ feedback during stance to assay anti-gravity thrust and phase timing, and silence Renshaw cells to test synergy stabilization, converting the review's catalog into lesion experiments.
robot_sim: Implement spindle (length/velocity), tendon-organ (force), and Renshaw recurrent feedback in a neuromuscular locomotion model and ablate each pathway to test the review's functional catalog: phase timing, fatigue compensation, linearization, and synergy stabilization.

title: In mice lacking V2a interneurons, gait depends on speed of locomotion
notes: Ablating V2a interneurons (Chx10::DTA mice) leaves slow-speed trot intact but shifts high-speed gait to synchronous left-right coupling without altering foreleg-hindleg alternation or swing/stance durations, a speed-specific loss of left-right alternation recapitulated in isolated-cord fictive locomotion, establishing V2a neurons as required for maintaining alternation at fast speeds.
animal_study: Test whether naturally galloping or hopping animals have reduced or modified V2a function (as the abstract poses), and optogenetically reactivate V2a neurons at high speed in Chx10::DTA mice to test whether left-right alternation can be restored.
robot_sim: Implement a speed-dependent commissural (V2a-analog) pathway that maintains left-right alternation at high frequencies; remove it and test whether the model transitions from alternate to synchronous gait as drive increases while sagittal timing is preserved.

title: Microstimulation of the medullary reticular formation during fictive locomotion.
notes: Microstimulation of the medullary reticular formation during fictive locomotion evokes site-dependent modulation of extensor activity — reticulospinal effects are state-dependent.

title: Peeling back the layers of locomotor control in the spinal cord
notes: Synthesizes optical and genetic work in mice and zebrafish into a layered picture of spinal locomotor control: modular spinal networks simplify limb and axial motor pool coordination, module deployment is reconfigured with increasing locomotor speed, and rhythm and pattern are regulated in functional hierarchies.
animal_study: Use intersectional genetic ablation of specific modules at defined locomotor speeds in mice or zebrafish larvae to test whether module removal produces the predicted speed-dependent coordination deficits and hierarchy reorganization.
robot_sim: Build a hierarchical controller with rhythm and pattern layers plus speed-dependent module recruitment; ablate modules at specific speeds to test the modularity and hierarchy claims drawn from mice and zebrafish.

title: Generation of human bipedal locomotion by a bio-mimetic neuro-musculo-skeletal model.
notes: A neuro-musculo-skeletal biped model (seven sagittal links, nine muscles, per-muscle spindle, Golgi tendon organ, and alpha-motoneuron units) whose reflex connection weights are optimized with a genetic algorithm reproduces human walking remarkably well, attributing the emergent gait largely to reciprocal spindle innervation interacting with musculoskeletal mechanics rather than detailed central programming.
animal_study: Test the model's reliance on peripheral reflexes through staged deafferentation in locomoting animals, predicting graded pattern degradation as spindle and tendon-organ feedback weights are removed while central drive is held constant.
robot_sim: Replicate the architecture: per-muscle spindle, tendon-organ, and alpha-motoneuron units converging with foot-contact and rhythm-generator input, weights optimized for walking distance and energy; ablate spindle versus tendon-organ channels to quantify their contribution to the emergent gait.

title: Interlimb communication during human walking: crossed responses in the gastrocnemius muscle
notes: Thesis work mapping interlimb neural pathways between the gastrocnemii during human walking: building on the short-latency crossed response documented in soleus, it investigates crossed responses in the gastrocnemius as evidence that spinal interlimb coordination circuits, well documented in animals, operate in humans under supraspinal control.

title: The cat step cycle: Hind limb joint angles and muscle lengths during unrestrained locomotion
notes: The reference cat hindlimb kinematics dataset: from walking to galloping the F/E1/E2/E3 phase sequence is preserved while E3 compresses most and F expands, knee and ankle move in near unity, and stance extensors undergo a single stretch-shorten cycle, implying muscle spindles and tendon organs are driven primarily by lengthening and isometric contractions rather than passive stretch, with synchronous activation of Ia, group II, and Ib endings as muscles become active.
animal_study: Record muscle spindle Ia/II and tendon organ Ib afferents in freely moving cats across the walk-to-gallop speed range to test the predicted dominance of lengthening and isometric contractions in driving afferent discharge and the synchronous activation of Ia, II, and Ib endings.
robot_sim: Use the F/E1/E2/E3 phase-duration scaling and knee-ankle unity as kinematic targets across speeds, and drive afferent models from lengthening/isometric contraction phases rather than absolute length to reproduce natural spindle and tendon-organ activation timing.

title: V1 spinal neurons regulate the speed of vertebrate locomotor outputs.
notes: Genetically silencing V1 interneurons (Engrailed1-expressing inhibitory cells) eliminates fast motor bursting during locomotion, establishing local inhibition as the element that sets locomotor CPG cycle frequency and positioning V1 neurons as an evolutionarily conserved speed-control pathway for vertebrate locomotor movements.
animal_study: Test the claimed evolutionary conservation directly: silence V1-equivalent inhibitory populations in zebrafish or lamprey and test whether fast bursting selectively drops while slow rhythms persist, as in mouse.
robot_sim: Add an inhibitory V1-analog population to a half-center CPG whose gain sets burst frequency; ablating it should selectively remove fast motor bursting while slower rhythms persist, separating speed control from rhythm generation.

title: Motor antagonism exposed by spatial segregation and timing of neurogenesis
notes: Extensor and flexor premotor interneurons are segregated medio-laterally in the dorsal spinal cord yet derive from common progenitor domains separated only by timing of neurogenesis, and proprioceptive feedback selectively targets the medial extensor premotor population, where it is required for extensor-specific connectivity to develop — an anatomical and developmental basis for antagonistic circuitry.
animal_study: Neonatal dorsal-root section or genetic elimination of muscle spindles at different developmental stages, followed by trans-synaptic viral mapping of premotor connectivity, would test whether proprioceptive input is instructive for extensor premotor organization or merely permissive.
robot_sim: Route proprioceptive feedback preferentially onto the extensor premotor side of a bilateral CPG and remove it during connection formation to test whether extensor-specific connectivity fails to develop, mirroring the developmental requirement.

title: Common interneurones in reflex pathways from group 1a and 1b afferents of ankle extensors in the cat.
notes: Most lamina V-VI interneurones take convergent input from both Ia spindle and Ib tendon-organ afferents of ankle and toe extensors — about 64% shared pathways showing co-excitation, co-inhibition, or opposite actions — so reflex circuitry is not strictly partitioned between length and force feedback, and interneurones projecting to motor nuclei show the same convergence.

title: Afferent control of locomotor CPG: insights from a simple neuromechanical model
notes: In a single-joint neuromechanical model, length (Ia, II) and extensor force (Ib) feedback entrain the CPG to limb dynamics and produce the extensor-dominated speed regulation of real locomotion — higher drive shortens stance while swing stays nearly constant, an asymmetry absent from the CPG's fictive pattern — and increasing afferent weights restores stable locomotion after supraspinal drive removal, mechanistically modeling locomotor training after spinal cord injury.
animal_study: Test the training prediction in spinal-transected animals: treadmill training with augmented versus reduced extensor load feedback (robotic stance loading, or deafferented controls) should speed or slow recovery of stepping, probing whether recovery acts through increased afferent input weights.
robot_sim: Implement the two-muscle single-joint CPG with Ia/II length and extensor Ib force feedback; sweep drive to verify stance-only shortening, ablate afferents to collapse speed regulation to the intrinsic fictive pattern, and raise afferent weights to emulate post-SCI training recovery.

title: Neural networks that co-ordinate locomotion and body orientation in lamprey
notes: Lamprey networks coordinating locomotion and body orientation; the lamprey as the reference preparation for cellular-level CPG and reticulospinal control.

title: On a response characteristic of a mathematical neuron model
CONTROL OF LOCOMOTION IN THE DECEREBRATE CAT
feedback: Ia or II stance to swing
notes: In the decerebrate cat, locomotion is initiated by the mesencephalic locomotor region acting through the medial medullary reticular formation and the ventrolateral funiculus, and the phase transitions are set by identified afferents: group I Golgi tendon organ afferents prolong stance, while length- and velocity-sensitive afferents from extensor muscles signal leg extension to permit swing — unloaded and extended is the swing-permitting state.

title: Functional identification of interneurons responsible for left-right coordination of hindlimbs in mammals.
notes: Commissural interneurons organizing left-right hindlimb coordination form distinct rostral-lumbar flexor and extensor centers that define activity in caudal flexor and extensor motor pools across the midline, with some connections functionally reconfigured when switching from rest to locomotion — a candidate substrate for state-dependent spinal synaptic plasticity.
animal_study: Test whether the rest-to-locomotion reconfiguration of commissural connections is activity-dependent: pharmacologically block locomotor-like activity during the transition in the neonatal cord preparation and re-assess commissural inputs onto identified motor pools.
robot_sim: Implement distinct flexor and extensor commissural centers driving contralateral caudal motor pools, with connection weights that switch between rest and locomotion states; ablating the commissural population should collapse left-right alternation.

title: Neuronal activity in the isolated mouse spinal cord during spontaneous deletions in fictive locomotion: insights into locomotor central pattern generator organization
notes:
Zhong, Shevtsova, Rybak.
Key points 
• The organization of the spinal circuitry responsible for the generation of locomotor rhythm and control of locomotion in mammals is largely unknown, though several types of spinal interneurons involved in the rodent locomotor network have been identified. 
• Ventral root recordings of spinal motoneurons during fictive locomotion in the isolated mouse spinal cord show spontaneous deletions of activity. The majority of deletions in the isolated neonatal mouse spinal cord are non-resetting: they do not change the phase of subsequent motor cycles. Flexor and extensor motoneurons express asymmetric responses during deletions: flexor deletions are accompanied by tonic ipsilateral extensor activity, while extensor deletions do not perturb rhythmic ipsilateral flexor activity. Non-resetting deletions on one side of the cord do not perturb rhythmic activity on the other side of the cord and can occur in isolated hemicords. 
• We have characterized the activity of motoneurons and identified interneurons during spontaneous motor deletions. The motoneurons and a subset of V2a interneurons fall silent during non-resetting motor deletions while a second subset of V2a interneurons and commissural interneurons continue unperturbed rhythmic firing. This allowed us to suggest their involvement at different levels of the locomotor network operation.
